title: Advanced Tactical Ordnance Systems, LLC v. Real Action Paintball, Inc.
lead: A PepperBall trademark purchaser sued a California rival in Indiana, but its evidence did not connect the rival’s Indiana customers to the allegedly misleading announcement.

actors.name: Advanced Tactical Ordnance Systems
actors.role: Acquirer of PepperBall trademarks and other property, asserting an Indiana headquarters.

actors.name: Real Action Paintball and K.T. Tran
actors.role: California company and its president, sued over marketing of irritant projectiles.

actors.name: APON
actors.role: Mexican projectile supplier whose California-based chief operating officer arranged the Real Action deal.

proceedings: The Northern District of Indiana found personal jurisdiction after an evidentiary hearing and issued a preliminary injunction. The Seventh Circuit remanded for vacatur of that injunction and dismissal for lack of personal jurisdiction.
limits: Trademark liability and the substantive injunction requirements were not decided. The appellate court questioned, rather than established, Advanced Tactical’s asserted Indiana headquarters. The May 12 correction identifies the preliminary injunction as the relief to vacate.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A foreclosure sale changes the PepperBall business
paragraphs: Advanced Tactical Ordnance Systems manufactured PepperBall products, irritant-filled projectiles resembling pepper spray sold mainly to police departments, security firms, and similar customers. In a 2012 foreclosure sale it acquired the trademarks and other property of California-based PepperBall Technologies. Advanced Tactical asserted that its headquarters was in Indiana, although the appellate court noted uncertainty about that assertion and an apparent California office.

Before foreclosure, PepperBall Technologies obtained projectiles from Perfect Circle, a half owner of Advanced Tactical, and APON, a Mexican company. After the acquisition APON stopped manufacturing or assembling PepperBall projectiles. APON’s California-resident chief operating officer approached Real Action Paintball, a California company, about supplying irritant projectiles. They reached an agreement in August 2012.

sections.title: Real Action’s announcement prompts an Indiana lawsuit
paragraphs: Real Action posted a website notice and emailed subscribers saying it had acquired the machinery, recipes, and materials formerly used by PepperBall Technologies. Advanced Tactical complained that this misleadingly suggested Real Action was now the sole PepperBall manufacturer. After a cease-and-desist letter, Real Action added a disclaimer denying affiliation with PepperBall Technologies or its brands and stating that its projectiles were not made by the current company using that name.

Advanced Tactical remained dissatisfied and sued Real Action and its president, K.T. Tran, in the Northern District of Indiana. It asserted federal and common-law trademark infringement, unfair competition, trade-dress infringement, and trade-secret misappropriation. The appeal treated the company and Tran together because no material difference between them mattered there; this did not establish either one’s liability.

To support Indiana jurisdiction, Advanced Tactical pointed to an interactive ordering website, email blasts reaching Indiana, Indiana sales revenue, foreseeable in-state injury from out-of-state torts, and an alleged conspiracy to harm an Indiana business. Real Action preserved its jurisdictional objection. After a December 7, 2012 evidentiary hearing, the district court found jurisdiction and granted a preliminary injunction.

sections.title: The injunction appeal requires resolving the court’s power
paragraphs: Real Action appealed the injunction and jurisdiction ruling under 28 U.S.C. § 1292(a)(1). Advanced Tactical argued that personal jurisdiction fell outside that interlocutory appeal; Real Action invoked pendent appellate jurisdiction. Chief Judge Wood, writing with Judges Posner and Kanne, rejected both descriptions. A court could not validly enjoin a defendant over whom it lacked jurisdiction, making the preserved objection an essential threshold part of reviewing the injunction. Although personal jurisdiction could be waived, it had not been waived here.

Because the district court had held an evidentiary hearing, Advanced Tactical had to establish jurisdiction by a preponderance of the evidence, rather than the prima facie showing that might suffice on written submissions. The Lanham Act supplied no special jurisdictional rule. Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 4(k)(1)(A) therefore led to Indiana’s long-arm provision, which extended to federal due-process limits. Advanced Tactical conceded the absence of general jurisdiction. Federal subject-matter jurisdiction did not answer the separate question of power over these defendants; specific jurisdiction required their suit-related Indiana conduct.

sections.title: Sales and injury do not establish the missing connection
paragraphs: The Supreme Court’s recent Walden decision emphasized that the defendant’s conduct must connect the forum and the litigation. The plaintiff’s forum location and foreseeable injury there could not be the only link, even for intentional torts.

The district court had relied on several Indiana orders filled after the challenged announcement. But Advanced Tactical showed neither that those purchasers had seen the announcement before ordering nor that it had misled them about the PepperBall manufacturer. Allegations of more than six hundred Indiana sales over two years did not supply the missing relationship to this wrong. The defect was not a categorical rule against jurisdiction based on a small number of sales; it was failure to connect relevant transactions to the alleged misconduct. Otherwise inadequately linked shipments could expose a seller to litigation wherever an item arrived.

Real Action’s knowledge of Advanced Tactical’s asserted Indiana location likewise showed only possible injury to a forum-connected plaintiff. The circuit acknowledged tension in its own earlier decisions but explained that any interpretation making the plaintiff the sole forum link could not survive Walden.

sections.title: Online availability does not show deliberate Indiana targeting
paragraphs: The subscriber list’s inclusion of Indiana recipients did not show deliberate cultivation of Indiana for the allegedly misleading message. Email users could send and open messages wherever they happened to be; their subscription decisions and postal addresses did not automatically create substantial connections to every listed state. The economic value of subscribers did not identify the necessary deliberate Indiana connection.

Geographically restricted advertising might supply different evidence of targeting, but Advanced Tactical introduced no comparable evidence and made no such appellate argument. The court did not rule that email could never support jurisdiction or that online advertising always would. Website interactivity was also a poor substitute for a forum-specific connection. The challenged announcement was simply a posted notice; other interactive features did not connect it to Indiana. Ordinary due-process principles could address Internet conduct without a categorical Internet test. The court recognized that Walden itself had reserved virtual-contact questions and applied those principles through the circuit’s own Internet precedents.

On May 9, 2014 the Seventh Circuit remanded with instructions to vacate the preliminary injunction and dismiss the complaint for lack of personal jurisdiction. A May 12 correction expressly identified the preliminary injunction as the relief to vacate. The court did not decide trademark infringement or the substantive grounds for an injunction. No separate opinion was filed.
